scope: test the address hypothesis with the address armed before the gamestate

verified_facts.forward_reached_server: connect logged, stats logged, three fragments emitted (seq 3, index 0/1/2)

conclusion.address_hypothesis_rejected: even with address_string set to 'localhost' and all five injected datagrams consumed (ring_b 5/5), the client did not advance stage or messageAck
conclusion.so: a mismatched peer address is not what blocks acceptance; at minimum it is not the only blocker, and our synthetic connection is consumed regardless of connection_adr

cumulative_exclusions: fragment header, count, stride, chunk, sequence sharing and start value
transport and consumption (ring_b read == write every run)

what_remains.inside_client_after_ring_read: the client reads the datagram from ring B but the datagram never becomes an accepted message
candidate_causes: the client's reader expects the datagram to arrive through its own socket path (recvfrom) and the ring injection bypasses a state machine step that the normal path sets
the netchan sequence numbers it tracks (incomingSequence/outgoingAcknowledgement) diverge from the ones our packets carry, so every packet looks out of order
a reliable-command layer expects a specific first message that we never send

highest_value_next_step.idea: read the client's netchan sequence fields (incomingSequence / outgoingSequence for the game connection) and compare them with the sequence we put on the wire (3)
highest_value_next_step.why: if the client's incomingSequence is not 2 (expecting 3 next), our datagrams are dropped as out-of-order before payload parsing - which would explain every rejection regardless of content
highest_value_next_step.how: scan the game connection object for small int pairs near the address struct, or reuse any existing netchan field offset knowledge from the 2697 work
